# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up does what the earlier papers asked for. It uses record-based output, two measures of actual hours, a randomised comparison, two years of data, and a mediation test registered in advance. It also corrects the meta-analysis's decay claim with information the meta-analysis didn't disclose. The arithmetic holds. The main issues are that the "decay" estimate is confounded by changes in the control offices, and that the meetings mediation is partly an accounting identity. Some of the Summary's wording is also stronger than the body supports.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Reported | Computed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets (0.966 / 0.88) | +9.8% | +9.8% | ✓ |
| Per hour, logs (0.966 / 0.89) | +8.5% | +8.5% | ✓ |
| CIs carried through the hours ratio | 4.6–15.2; 3.4–13.8 | ≈4.5–15.0; 3.4–13.7 | ✓ |
| Decline on the timesheet measure (12.5 → 9.8) | "about a quarter" | −22% | ✓ |
| Mediation shares (47 + 18 + 35) | 100% | 100% | ✓ |
| Halden hours 40.3 → 34.9 | −13.4% | −13.4% | ✓ |
| Halden per hour (96.8 / 86.6) | +11.8% | +11.8% | ✓ |

## 1. Part of the "decay" may be the control group improving

Two control offices cut their meetings in month 15. Their output per hour then rose about 4.1%. Spread across seven control offices, that raises the control average by about 1.2 points, which lowers the difference-in-differences at 24 months by roughly the same amount. So close to half of the timesheet decline from 12.5% to 9.8% could reflect contamination of the control group rather than treated offices falling back. The authors don't make this connection.

The paper should report treated and control trends separately. It should also re-estimate the effect with the two audit offices excluded, or with their post-audit months excluded, as a sensitivity check. Monthly series would also show whether the gain is levelling off or still falling. With only two time points, 9 and 24 months, you can't tell.

The control meetings figures also look odd. The control average moved only from 7.2 to 7.0 hours, yet two of the seven offices fell by about 2.1 hours each. If offices are weighted equally, the other five must have *increased* by about 0.5 hours each. That's possible, but it needs a word of explanation, or it reflects weighting by staff numbers.

## 2. The meetings mediation is close to an accounting identity

Meeting time is part of working hours, so cutting meetings mechanically raises output per hour if output holds. A rough decomposition with the timesheet figures shows how much this matters. It assumes control hours stayed stable at about 37.9:

| | Pre: total | Pre: meetings | Pre: non-meeting | Month 24: total | Month 24: meetings | Month 24: non-meeting |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | 37.9 | 7.4 | 30.5 | ~33.4 | 3.9 | ~29.5 |
| Control | ~37.9 | 7.2 | ~30.7 | ~37.9 | 7.0 | ~30.9 |

Non-meeting hours fell about 4% relative to control, and output fell 3.4%. **Output per non-meeting hour is essentially unchanged, around +1%.** On this rough decomposition, removing meeting time accounts for nearly all of the per-hour gain, not 47%. That leaves little room for the 18% attributed to fatigue or the 35% left unexplained.

Two things follow:

- **The definition of the log measure matters.** If "active log-in time" covers only case-system work and excludes meetings, an 11% fall is hard to reconcile with meetings falling 3.5 hours and total hours falling about 4.5. If logs include meetings, the log-based mediation is partly mechanical. The paper should say what the log measure includes and report a decomposition like the one above.
- **The real finding is substantive but different.** About 3.5 hours of weekly meetings were removed with no measurable loss of output or quality: overturn rates were 3.2% against 3.0%. That shows the meetings were of low value. It is not the same as "meetings explain 47% of a productivity effect." I'd present it as removing low-value time, which is what the nine-month report suggested.

## 3. Mediation inference

- **The effective sample is 14 offices, not office-months.** Office-months are not independent. A mediation share of 47% with a CI of 28–66% looks narrow when the total effect's own CI runs from 3.4% to 13.8%. Confirm that the CIs account for clustering with this few clusters, for example with a cluster bootstrap.
- **This is confirmation within the same sample, not replication.** The hypothesis came from these same seven offices at month 6, and the analysis was registered at month 11 with months 1 to 11 already observed. Registration still has value, but it is not an independent test. That partly answers the re-analysis's "post hoc" objection, but not fully.
- **"Confirms" in the Summary overclaims.** Mediation depends on there being no unmeasured confounding of the mediator–outcome link. The Limitations section says so, and the body says "survives." For example, better-run offices could both cut meetings more and produce more. "Confirms" should be softened to match.

## 4. The Summary is inconsistent with the body

- **It mixes measures when describing the decline.** "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares the nine-month timesheet figure with the 24-month log figure. That makes the decline look like a third. The like-for-like comparison, 12.5% to 9.8%, is about a fifth, as the body says. The Summary should use that, or report both measures at 24 months.
- **"All with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the evidence.** One of the three organisations that reverted was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Under the meta-analysis's coding, deadline-driven work is *discretionary*. So one discretionary organisation also reverted, with output at 88–91. That's worth stating plainly rather than folding into the coverage story.

## 5. Counter-arm cost figure

Restoring service needed 12% more staff, yet cost per contact rises only 9%. If staff costs scale fully, cost per contact should rise about 12–13%. A 9% figure fits if staff are about three-quarters of total costs. Please state the assumption. This is the clearest cost figure across all five papers, so it should be traceable.

The arm ending at month 12 also matters for interpretation. Long-run evidence on coverage-bound work now consists only of organisations that chose to continue.

## 6. Halden subset

- **Non-response.** 14 of 23 organisations agreed to take part. The nine that didn't are the likeliest to include further reversions. Reversion among the 14 (3 of 14) is therefore a lower bound.
- **Hours data and baseline.** Varga & Holm found only 17 organisations with both records and time tracking. Do all 11 continuing organisations have time tracking? Is the 40.3 baseline specific to these 11? It equals the mean for Varga & Holm's 27 time-tracking organisations exactly, which may be a coincidence but should be confirmed.
- **The framing is appropriate.** Calling this "an upper bound for organisations that self-select … and find it suits them" is the right way to present it. The six-month seasonal-baseline problem also remains for these comparisons.
- **The attrition question goes unanswered.** Varga & Holm showed that seven of nine Halden withdrawals happened after the schedule began, contrary to the original working paper. A Halden author co-signs this report, which would be the natural place to correct or explain the original account. It isn't mentioned.

## 7. Smaller points

- **The rebuttals are mostly fair.**
  - Against "entirely an artifact": the Varden estimate meets the re-analysis's own stated standards and excludes zero.
  - Against "no sign of decay": the disclosure that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled with scheduled hours supports what I suspected earlier.
  - "Not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten" is fair. Note, though, that the energy extrapolation used Halden data, not Varden data.
- **Resignations and quality are still raw comparisons without CIs**, as in the nine-month report.
- **The meeting-audit observation is reported with good restraint.** Saying no arm reorganised without cutting hours points to the obvious next trial: a three-arm design with reduced hours, reorganisation only, and control.
- **Conflict of interest.** Authors evaluating their own trial and their own pilot, and responding to critics, should be stated in a disclosure. That is standard practice and doesn't imply bias.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Real and lasting to 24 months, roughly 8–10%. Some decline from 9 months, but part of that may be control contamination. |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Slightly below control, around −3%. The hours cut is mostly but not fully offset. |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per worker falls about 10%. Service worsens. Restoring it costs more. One randomised arm was stopped. |
| Mechanism | Mostly removing low-value meeting time. Fatigue contributes modestly at most. |
| Is the hours cut necessary? | Unknown. The meeting-audit offices suggest some of the gain is available without it, but this is uncontrolled and based on two offices. |
| Original Halden headline (+23.4%, sector-general) | Not supported on either count. |

I can draft a referee report, write a short synthesis across all five documents, or sketch the three-arm design that would test whether the hours cut is necessary.
